{{Short description|Austrian-American mathematician (1928-2017)}}
'''Hans F. Weinberger''' (September 27, 1928 in [[Vienna]] – September 15, 2017 in [[Durham, North Carolina]])<ref>[http://www.math.umn.edu/~hfw/ homepage]</ref> was an [[Austrians|Austrian]]-[[United States|American]] [[mathematician]], known for his contributions
to [[variational methods]] for [[eigenvalue]] problems, [[partial differential equations]], and [[fluid dynamics]].

He obtained an [[Master of Science|M.S.]] in [[physics]] from [[Carnegie Institute of Technology]] (1948) where he also got his [[Sc.D.]] on the
thesis ''Fourier Transforms of Moebius Series'' advised by [[Richard Duffin]] (1950).<ref>{{MathGenealogy|10297}}</ref>
He then worked at the institute for Fluid Dynamics at [[University of Maryland, College Park]] (1950&ndash;60),
and as [[professor]] at [[University of Minnesota]] (1961&ndash;98) where he was department head (1967&ndash;69) and
now is Professor Emeritus (1998&ndash;).  Weinberger was the first director of [[Institute for Mathematics and its Applications]] (1981&ndash;87). Weinberger served as the IMA's first director from 1982 to 1987, and under his leadership, the IMA quickly became known for cutting-edge scientific programs, a collaborative atmosphere, and as a training ground for postdoctoral researchers. During his tenure, Weinberger was very engaged in scientific life at the IMA, attending lectures and collaborating with visitors and postdocs. His presence at these lectures usually meant that the toughest and most penetrating questions were asked.

While well known for his contributions to the analysis of partial differential equations, especially eigenvalue problems, Weinberger turned his attention to mathematical biology later in his career. He remained active in research throughout his life and authored several papers after his retirement in 1998. Weinberger was elected a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1986 and was in the inaugural class of the American Mathematical Society Fellows in 2012 [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved 2013-09-01.</ref>
